questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient sustains a traumatic injury resulting in damage to nervous tissue. The subsequent healing process involves the formation of scar tissue at the site of injury. Which of the following cell types is primarily responsible for the formation of scar tissue during the repair of nervous tissue?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option B: Fibroblasts are the primary cell type responsible for scar formation in peripheral tissues, but not typically within the CNS, as they produce collagen and other extracellular matrix components leading to the formation of connective tissue scars.

 

Option C: Axons do not form scar tissue but can be involved in the regeneration process in the peripheral nervous system under certain conditions.

 

Option D: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS, involved in the immune response and clean-up after injury but are not the primary cells responsible for scar tissue formation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The cell type primarily responsible for the formation of scar tissue during the repair of nervous tissue is Neuroglia, as astrocytes, a type of glial cell, play a crucial role in the gliosis process that leads to scar formation in the CNS.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1255



Robbins 10th 1255

questions.stem: A 75-year-old patient presents to the neurology clinic with a progressive decline in memory and cognitive function over the past few years. The family reports episodes of visual hallucinations and fluctuations in alertness. Cognitive testing demonstrates impaired memory recall and difficulty with executive functions. An MRI of the brain shows atrophy in the temporal and parietal lobes. Biopsy of brain tissue was done. Which of the following features is not typically associated with the pathology of this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
g>: These are twisted tangles of tau protein within nerve cells.

 

Option B: Senile (neuritic) plaques: These are abnormal clusters of beta-amyloid protein that accumulate between nerve cells.

 

Option C: Amyloid angiopathy: It involves the deposition of amyloid protein in blood vessel walls.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lewy bodies are not typically associated with the pathology of Alzheimer's disease, which is characterized by neurofibrillary tangles, senile neuritic plaques, and amyloid angiopathy.

 

Lewy bodies are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions composed of alpha-synuclein, seen in:

 

  • Parkinson’s disease
  • Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)

 

Ref: Robbins 10th / 1275



Robbins 10th / 1275

questions.stem: A 68-year-old patient presents with a gradual decline in memory and cognitive function over the past few years. Family members report increasing forgetfulness and difficulty with daily tasks. Neurological examination reveals no tremors or rigidity but does show signs of impaired memory recall. An MRI of the brain demonstrates atrophy in the temporal and parietal lobes. Biopsy of brain tissue reveals neurofibrillary tangles. Which condition is the patient likely to be suffering?
questions.solutionHtml:
2.0pt">Explanation:

 

Option A: Parkinson's disease is characterized by the presence of Lewy bodies, not neurofibrillary tangles.

 

Option C: Multiple sclerosis involves demyelination of nerve fibers and is not typically associated with neurofibrillary tangles.

 

Option D: Perivenous encephalomyelitis: It may refer to inflammation around blood vessels in the brain and spinal cord, but without more specific information, it's challenging to associate it with neurofibrillary tangles.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Alzheimer's disease is characterized by the presence of neurofibrillary tangles composed of tau protein within nerve cells, which are a hallmark of the disease's neuropathology.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1278

questions.stem: Dementia in an old man with senile plaques is usually associated with:
questions.solutionHtml:
n>

 

Option B: Pick's disease: Also known as frontotemporal dementia, is characterized by the presence of abnormal tau protein in nerve cells, but it is not typically associated with senile plaques.

 

Option C: Parkinson's disease: It primarily involves motor symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia. It is not directly associated with senile plaques.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1275

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of progressive memory loss and cognitive decline over the past 5 years is brought to the physician by his family due to concerns about his worsening ability to perform daily tasks. The patient's Mini-Mental State Examination score has declined significantly since the last visit. An MRI of the brain shows widespread atrophy with particular emphasis in the temporal and parietal lobes. Histological examination of a biopsy specimen from the cerebral cortex reveals extracellular amyloid deposits and intraneuronal hyperphosphorylated tau protein aggregates. Which of the following additional histopathological findings would be least likely to support the likely disease in the patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of granulovacuolar degeneration in hippocampal neurons

options.label: B
options.text: Abundant deposition of alpha-synuclein within neurons

options.label: C
options.text: Extensive amyloid deposition in the walls of cerebral blood vessels

options.label: D
options.text: Accumulation of Hirano bodies in the hippocampus

questions.answerText: Abundant deposition of alpha-synuclein within neurons
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-size:12.0pt;">Explanation:

 

Option A: Granulovacuolar degeneration is characterized by small fluid-filled cavities containing granular debris found in the hippocampal neurons and is often seen in Alzheimer's disease.

 

Option C: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy involves the deposition of amyloid-beta protein in the walls of small to medium-sized arteries in the central nervous system and is commonly associated with Alzheimer's disease.

 

Option D: Hirano bodies are intracellular inclusions found in the astrocytic processes that are often associated with Alzheimer's disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The least likely histopathological finding to support the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease is abundant deposition of alpha-synuclein within neurons, as this is indicative of disorders such as Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia, rather than Alzheimer's disease.

 

Typical histological features of Alzheimer disease:

 

  • Neuritic (senile) plaques: extracellular deposits of Aβ
  • Neurofibrillary tangles: intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau
  • Amyloid deposition in cerebral vessels: cerebral amyloid angiopathy → ↑ risk of hemorrhage
  • Granulovacuolar degeneration: cytoplasmic vacuoles in hippocampal neurons
  • Hirano bodies: eosinophilic, rod-shaped inclusions in hippocampus (actin & actin-associated proteins)

 

Summary:

 

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1275




Robbins 10th 1275

questions.stem: Tau protein are associated with all except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Huntington’s disease

 

Option D:

 

Tau protein is primarily associated with neurodegenerative disorders characterized by tauopathy, where abnormal tau protein aggregates are found in the brain. Huntington's disease, on the other hand, is characterized by the presence of abnormal huntingtin protein aggregates, not tau protein.

 

 

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1285

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient presents with a progressive decline in memory and cognitive function. Genetic testing reveals a polymorphism in the APOE gene, specifically the ε4 allele. This gene is implicated in the risk and susceptibility to late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Which chromosome harbours the APOE gene associated with Alzheimer's disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 19

 

Option D:

 

  • In familial Alzheimer disease and Down syndrome, the gene encoding APP on chromosome 21 is involved.
  • The genetic locus on chromosome 19 that encodes apolipoprotein E (ApoE) has a strong influence on the risk of developing AD.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The APOE gene associated with Alzheimer's disease is located on chromosome 19. This locus has a significant impact on the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's disease, particularly the ε4 allele.

 

Three common alleles: ε2, ε3, ε4

 

  • ε4 → increases risk & lowers age of onset
  • ε2 → may be protective

 

APOE’s main role: lipid transport and neuronal repair; also affects amyloid beta metabolism.

 

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1285

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male presents with a resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity. On examination, there is a characteristic "pill-rolling" tremor observed. The patient also exhibits postural instability. Which neurotransmitter is primarily affected in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
yle="font-size:11pt">Option A: Changes in serotonin levels are more associated with mood disorders.

 

Option B: While imbalances in acetylcholine and dopamine play a role in movement disorders, the primary deficit in Parkinson's disease is related to dopamine deficiency.

 

Option C: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, and alterations in GABAergic transmission are not the primary cause of Parkinson's disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The neurotransmitter primarily affected in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease is Dopamine, which is depleted due to degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to characteristic symptoms like resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1293



Robbins 10th 1293

questions.stem: Which of the following is affected in patients with Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
ontal lobes may be affected later in Alzheimer’s disease, they are not typically the regions most affected early in the disease process.

 

Option C: Temporal lobe involvement is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, but the occipital lobe is generally spared until the later stages of the disease.

 

Option D: The occipital lobe, involved in visual processing, is typically less affected than the parietal and temporal lobes in Alzheimer’s disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In Alzheimer’s disease, atrophy is most pronounced in the parietal and temporal lobes, which includes the hippocampus, one of the earliest and most severely affected areas.

 

Ref: Robbin 10th/ 1275



Robbin 10th/ 1275

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male presents with gait problems. On examination, a key pathological feature in the substantia nigra neurons is observed, characterized by abnormal protein aggregates primarily composed of alpha-synuclein. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the presence of these intracellular inclusions?
questions.solutionHtml:
planation:

 

Option A: While Alzheimer's disease may involve abnormal protein aggregates, including beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, Lewy bodies are not characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

 

Option C: Huntington's disease is characterized by the presence of huntingtin protein aggregates but not Lewy bodies.

 

Option D: Pick's disease is associated with frontotemporal lobar degeneration and is characterized by Pick bodies, not Lewy bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Parkinson disease is most likely responsible for the presence of these intracellular inclusions, as Lewy bodies composed of alpha-synuclein are a hallmark of this condition.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1282



Robbins 10th 1282

questions.stem: A 67-year-old male with a history of smoking and a recent diagnosis of small-cell lung carcinoma presents with a chief complaint of increasing weakness, particularly in the proximal muscles of his limbs. He reports that the weakness improves with repeated use of the muscles. Electromyography reveals a decremental response in muscle action potential amplitude with low-frequency stimulation, which improves with high-frequency stimulation. Mechanism of muscle weakness in Lambert-Eaton syndrome is which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Diminished calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum

options.label: C
options.text: Accelerated uptake of the neurotransmitter at the nerve-muscle junction

options.label: D
options.text: Antibody against presynaptic channels at the nerve-muscle junction

questions.answerText: Antibody against presynaptic channels at the nerve-muscle junction
questions.solutionHtml:
yle="font-size:12pt">Option A: Diminished calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum would affect muscle contraction but is not the mechanism of muscle weakness seen in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

 

Option B: An antibody against the sarcoplasmic reticulum is not associated with Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Antibodies in LEMS are directed against voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic nerve terminal, not against the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

 

Option C: Accelerated uptake of neurotransmitter at the nerve-muscle junction would likely lead to a decrease in available neurotransmitter for muscle contraction, but this is not the pathophysiology of Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Muscle weakness in Lambert-Eaton syndrome is due to antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels at the nerve-muscle junction, impairing acetylcholine release.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1226



Robbins 10th 1226

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient presents with headaches and visual disturbances. Imaging reveals a suprasellar mass consistent with a craniopharyngioma. The patient is concerned about the potential spread of the tumor. Which of the following brain tumors is least likely to spread via cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?
questions.solutionHtml:
e="font-size:11pt">Option B: Medulloblastoma is a highly malignant primary brain tumor that often spreads via the CSF, characteristically leading to drop metastasis at the cauda equina.

 

Option C: CNS lymphoma, although primarily a parenchymal brain tumor, can occasionally disseminate in the CSF, particularly in the setting of leptomeningeal disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Craniopharyngioma is the brain tumor that is least likely to spread via cerebrospinal fluid, as it typically presents with local growth and does not commonly disseminate through the CSF pathways.

 

Brain tumors spreading via CSF are

 

  • Ependymoma 
  • Medulloblastoma
  • Choroid plexus carcinoma
  • Astrocytoma
  • Germinoma
  • Pineoblastoma
  • CNS Lymphoma.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1293



Robbins 10th/ 1293

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old patient presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and persistent tinnitus. Physical examination reveals a non-tender mass in the vicinity of cranial nerve VIII. An MRI indicates a well-circumscribed mass in the internal acoustic meatus, and a subsequent biopsy is performed. Histologically, the tissue demonstrates distinct regions of cellularity with areas showing dense proliferation of spindle cells, while others show less density. There is also evidence of nuclear palisading. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
ly:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

 

Option B: Lymphoma: Lymphomas are neoplasms of the lymphatic system and would present histologically with an infiltration of lymphoid cells, which does not correspond to the nuclear palisading and alternating cellularity described in the stem.

 

Option C: Leukemia: This is a hematopoietic stem cell malignancy primarily affecting the bone marrow and blood. Histology of a solid mass would not reveal the characteristic findings of leukemia, such as blasts or excessive leukocytes.

 

Option D: Angiofibroma: Angiofibroma, often a benign tumor of adolescent males, would show a stromal and vascular component histologically, which is not described in the biopsy findings of the question stem.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The characteristic histological features of schwannomas are Antoni A areas, with hypercellular tissue and nuclear palisading, and Antoni B areas, which are less cellular.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/e p1237



Robbins 10th/e p1237

questions.stem: Which of the following receptor on neuronal membrane that induces development of glioma?
questions.solutionHtml:
ng>

 

Option A: CD45 is a common leukocyte antigen and is not specifically associated with glioma development.

 

Option C: CD33 is a cell surface marker associated with myeloid cells and is not directly related to glioma development.

 

Option D: CD24 is a cell adhesion molecule and has been associated with various cellular processes, but it is not a primary marker for glioma development.

 

Educational Objective:

 

CD133 is a marker associated with neural stem cells and is implicated in the tumorigenic properties of glioma stem cells, which contribute to the development of gliomas.

questions.stem: Which is not a neuronal tumor?
questions.solutionHtml:
ont-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option B: Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor derived from primitive neuroblasts, which are cells in the sympathetic nervous system, and it is indeed a neuronal tumor.

 

Option C: Gangliocytoma is a rare, benign tumor composed of mature neurons, and it is classified as a neuronal tumor.

 

Option D: Ganglioglioma is a tumor that contains both neoplastic neurons and glial cells, which classifies it as a mixed neuronal-glial tumor.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ependymoma is not a neuronal tumor; it is a glial tumor arising from the ependymal cells of the ventricular system.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1296



Robbins 10th/ 1296

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient presents with new-onset headaches, visual disturbances, and seizures. Brain imaging reveals multiple metastatic lesions. Which primary malignancy is most commonly associated with brain metastases in adults?
questions.solutionHtml:
p> 

Explanation:

 

Option A: While stomach cancer can metastasize to various organs, it is not the most common source of brain metastases in adults.

 

Option B: Ovarian cancer typically spreads to peritoneal surfaces and although it can metastasize widely, it is not the most frequent cause of brain metastases.

 

Option C: Oral cavity cancers tend to spread locally and to regional lymph nodes; they less commonly metastasize to the brain.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lung cancer is the primary malignancy most commonly associated with brain metastases in adults, reflecting both its prevalence and its biological behaviour of spreading to the brain.

 

The classic list to remember:

 

Lung > breast > melanoma > colon > kidney

 

  • Lung cancer is by far the most common cause of brain metastases in adults.
  • Breast is second.
  • Melanoma, kidney (renal cell carcinoma), and colon also metastasize to the brain.
  • Brain metastases from GI tumors like stomach or from ovary or oral cavity are much less common.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1301

The mass is excised and diagnosed as a schwannoma. Four years later, he presents with headaches and is found to have two meningiomas. Of the following, what is the most likely mutation that he possesses?

pan style="font-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Option C:

Explanation:

Option A. Mutations of PTEN are associated with colonic adenocarcinoma, breast and thyroid tumors.

Option B. Mutations of CDKN2 are associated with familial melanoma

Option D. Mutations of WT are associated with Wilms tumor

  • NF1, neurofibromin 1, is a tumor suppressor gene found on chromosome 17q11.2

The NF2 gene encodes a protein called merlin or schwannomin and is associated with Neurofibromatosis type II, which is characterized by multiple central nervous system tumors including schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about medulloblastoma?
questions.solutionHtml:
nt-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option A: Medulloblastoma is a radiosensitive tumor and radiation therapy is often part of the treatment plan.

 

Option B: Medulloblastoma commonly spreads through the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to leptomeningeal dissemination.

 

Option D: Medulloblastoma predominantly occurs in the pediatric age group.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Surgical treatment is indeed performed for medulloblastoma and it is an important part of the management strategy for this type of tumor.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1298

questions.stem: A 58-year-old patient presents with neurological symptoms, and imaging reveals multiple intracranial lesions. Considering all tumor types, which is the most common cause of intracranial tumors in adults?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A: Astrocytoma, which includes glioblastoma multiforme, is a type of primary brain tumor originating from astrocytes. They are one of the most common primary brain tumors in adults but not the most common cause of intracranial tumors when all tumor types are considered.

 

Option B: Medulloblastoma is a common brain tumor in children and is rarely the cause of intracranial tumors in adults, as its occurrence decreases significantly with age.

 

Option C: Meningiomas are common, usually benign, primary brain tumors arising from the meninges and are more prevalent in adults, particularly in women. However, they are not the most common cause of all intracranial tumors in adults.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Secondaries are the most common cause of intracranial tumors in adults, with metastases to the brain from other primary cancers occurring more frequently than primary brain tumors.
  • Common primaries that metastasize to the brain: lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, and colon.
  • Often multiple lesions, located at the gray-white matter junction.
  • Account for 40–50% of intracranial tumors in adults.
  • Among primary brain tumors in adults:
    • Most common benign → Meningioma
    • Most common malignant → Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM, an astrocytoma subtype)

questions.stem: Glial fibrillary proteins are present in:
questions.solutionHtml:
g>Option B: Medulloblastoma is a type of primitive neuroectodermal tumor that arises in the cerebellum and is not typically associated with GFAP, as it does not arise from glial cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

GFAP-

 

  • It is an intermediate filament protein
  • Marker of glial origin, mainly:
    • Astrocytes
    • Other glial-derived cells (including ependymal cells and certain oligodendrocytes)

 

Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is a marker for astrocytes and ependymal cells as well.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1293



Robbins 10th 1293

questions.stem: Enamel like superstructure is seen in which of the following neurological lesion?
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>Option B: Pituitary tumors typically do not present with enamel-like superstructures.

 

Option C: Astrocytomas are gliomas, and their appearance does not typically include enamel-like structures.

 

Option D: Ependymonas do not have the presence of enamel-like structure.

 

Educational Objective:

 

An enamel-like superstructure is characteristic of craniopharyngioma, a tumor that arises from Rathke’s pouch remnants and can show calcifications that resemble enamel.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1293



erred to as "calcification," is a characteristic feature seen in craniopharyngiomas. Craniopharyngiomas are tumors that arise from remnants of Rathke's pouch, an embryonic structure that contributes to pituitary development.

questions.stem: Pseudorosettes are seen in all except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A: Neuroblastoma is a pediatric tumor of the sympathetic nervous system and commonly displays pseudorosettes, where tumor cells are arranged around a fibrillary matrix but lack a true lumen.

 

Option B: Retinoblastoma, a malignant tumor of retinal cells, also can exhibit pseudorosette formation, where cells circle around a central area of necrosis or fibrillar material rather than a lumen. However, Retinoblastoma shows presence of both true as well as pseudo rosettes

 

Option C: Medulloblastoma is a primitive neuroectodermal tumor of the cerebellum in children and is characterized by the presence of pseudorosettes where the cells form perivascular patterns mimicking rosettes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pseudorosettes:

 

Arrangement of tumor cells around a central structure that is not a true lumen, usually around:

 

  • A blood vessel → perivascular pseudorosette

 

Seen in tumors of neuroectodermal origin

 

Pseudorosettes are typically seen in neuroblastoma, retinoblastoma, and medulloblastoma, but not in thecoma , which is an ovarian tumor.

 

Rosettes vs pseudorosettes:

 

 

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1293

questions.stem: Most common primary intracranial malignancy is:
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>, known for its poor prognosis and rapid progression.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: Ependymoma is a relatively rare glial tumor that arises from ependymal cells lining the ventricles or the central canal of the spinal cord and is more common in children and young adults.

 

Option C: Choroid angioma, also known as cavernous hemangioma, is a vascular malformation rather than a true neoplasm and is not considered a common cause of intracranial malignancy.

 

Option D: Pinealoma, or pineal gland tumor, is a rare type of brain tumor arising from the cells of the pineal gland; these can be benign or malignant but are not the most common brain tumors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glioblastoma is the most common intracranial malignancy, a highly aggressive and rapidly progressing tumor arising from astrocytes.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1294



Robbins 10th 1294

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female presents with a history of progressively worsening headaches and focal neurological deficits. Brain imaging reveals an enhancing mass which on histopathological examination confirms the diagnosis of meningioma. Which subtype of meningioma is associated with the worst prognosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-size:12pt">Option A: Syncytial meningiomas are characterized by densely packed cells with minimal intervening connective tissue.

 

Option B: Fibroblastic meningiomas are composed of spindle-shaped cells resembling fibroblasts.

 

Option D: Atypical meningiomas are intermediate in terms of aggressiveness between benign and anaplastic meningiomas.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Anaplastic meningioma is associated with the worst prognosis among the meningioma subtypes due to its high degree of cellular atypia and increased mitotic activity.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th /1301



Robbins 10th /1301

questions.stem: Which of the following is seen in schwannnoma?
questions.solutionHtml:
u>Explanation:

 

Option A. Spindle cells are indeed a component of schwannomas but are not specific to them as they can be seen in a variety of other neoplastic and reactive processes.

 

Option B. Storiform pattern, characterized by a cartwheel or mat-like arrangement of cells, is not typical for schwannoma. It's more commonly seen in dermatofibroma or malignant fibrous histiocytoma.

 

Option C. Target cells are a type of red blood cell with a bullseye appearance typically associated with conditions like liver disease or hemoglobinopathies, not schwannomas.

 

Educational objective:

 

Schwannomas are characterized by their distinctive Antoni A and B patterns on histology, which helps distinguish them from other soft tissue tumors. While spindle cells are a feature of schwannomas, the presence of the Antoni A and B patterns is more pathognomonic. Storiform patterns and target cells are associated with different pathologies and are not seen in schwannomas.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1302



Robbins 10th 1302

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with symptoms of vomiting, headache, and unsteady gait. Brain imaging reveals the diagnosis of a medulloblastoma. Which of the following is the commonest for this tumor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cerebellum

 

Option B:

 

Key points about medulloblastoma

 

  • In children, the location is in the midline of the cerebellum, but lateral locations are more often found in adults.
  • Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood
  • 5% of children have it in association with Gorlin syndrome (the most common of the inherited disorders due to mutations in the patched-1; PTCH-1 gene.
  • Histologically, there is presence of Homer-Wright rosettes.

 

Educational objective:

 

Medulloblastoma commonly occurs in the cerebellum , and is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1298



Robbins 10th 1298

questions.stem: In a pediatric patient diagnosed with a primitive neuroectodermal tumor of the cerebellum (medulloblastoma) , known for its aggressive nature and potential for metastasis, which anatomical site would be the most vigilant for the detection of metastatic spread?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) CNS

 

Option D:

 

Medulloblastomas have a propensity to spread to the subarachnoid space. Dissemination through the CSF is a common complication, giving rise to either extensive growth along the surface likened to “icing,” or nodular “drop metastases,” which tend to involve the cauda equina.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Medulloblastoma most commonly metastasizes within the central nervous system (CNS) , spreading through the CSF to create "drop metastases" particularly at the cauda equina.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1298



Robbins 10th 1298

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child presents with headaches and ataxia. Imaging reveals a cerebellar tumor with characteristic histological features, including the presence of eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped protein aggregates known as Rosenthal fibers. Which of the following tumors is most likely responsible for these histopathological findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
e="font-family:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

 

Option B: Glioblastomas are high-grade tumors that can have various cellular morphologies but do not typically have Rosenthal fibers as a defining characteristic.

 

Option C: Medulloblastomas are highly malignant primitive neuroectodermal tumors commonly found in the cerebellum of children but are not associated with Rosenthal fibers.

 

Option D: Ependymomas arise from the ependymal cells of the ventricular system and can occur in the cerebellum, but they are not characterized by the presence of Rosenthal fibers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pilocytic astrocytoma is most likely responsible for the histopathological findings of eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped Rosenthal fibers.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1293



Robbins 10th 1293

questions.stem: Verocay bodies are seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
ay exhibit whorled patterns and psammoma bodies, Verocay bodies are not a feature of meningiomas.

 

Option B: Hemangiomas are benign tumors derived from blood vessels and can occur in various tissues including the skin and internal organs. They do not display Verocay bodies.

 

Option C: Gliomas are tumors arising from glial cells in the central nervous system, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells. They do not have Verocay bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Verocay bodies are seen in schwannomas and are characterized by palisading nuclei creating nuclear-free zones within the densely cellular Antoni A areas of the tumor.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1302



erred to as Antoni A and Antoni B areas, respectively.

questions.stem: In reviewing brain imaging studies of various neoplasms, a physician notes the frequent occurrence of intratumoral calcifications. Such calcifications, though not exclusive, are most characteristically associated with which of the following types of primary brain tumors?
questions.solutionHtml:
-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A: Ependymomas, tumors arising from ependymal cells lining the ventricular system, can have various imaging features, but they are not specifically known for frequent calcification.

 

Option B: Medulloblastomas, which are malignant childhood tumors of the cerebellum, may show calcification, but it is not as common or pronounced as in oligodendrogliomas.

 

Option D: Glioblastomas are highly aggressive brain tumors that may occasionally show areas of calcification; however, calcifications are more characteristic and frequent in oligodendrogliomas.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Oligodendroglioma is the tumor most commonly associated with calcification in adult patients, a feature that can be visualized on imaging studies.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1295



Robbins 10th 1295

questions.stem: Which chromosome mutation is associated with medulloblastoma?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Chromosome 17

 

Option B:

 

Medulloblastomas have been associated with genetic abnormalities, and chromosome 17 abnormalities are frequently observed in these tumors. Specifically, mutations or deletions involving the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q) have been identified in a subset of medulloblastoma cases.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The chromosomal abnormalities associated with medulloblastomas, is seen due to mutations or deletions on chromosome 17.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th 1298

questions.stem: A neuropathologist is examining the brain from a patient with HIV, and, in the cerebral parenchyma, he identifies multinucleated cells. The virus is inducing a change in what type of cell to produce these giant cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
n style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Neurons are not typically the target cells for HIV replication.

 

Option B: Astrocytes are not the primary target cells for HIV replication; microglial cells play a more significant role.

 

Option C: Oligodendroglial cells are not the primary target cells for HIV; microglial cells are more commonly infected.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In HIV encephalitis, specifically microglial cells contribute in the formation of multinucleated giant cells within the cerebral parenchyma.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 1267

questions.solutionHtml:

Option B: Also known as Wilms' tumor, nephroblastoma is a kidney tumor usually found in children. It can show other types of rosette formations, but not typically Homer Wright rosettes.

 

Option C: Hepatoma, or hepatocellular carcinoma, is a liver tumor and does not feature the presence of Homer Wright rosettes. Its pathology is markedly different from that of neuroblastic tumors.

 

Option D: Ependymomas are glial cell tumors that can form rosettes known as perivascular rosettes or ependymal rosettes, which are distinct from Homer Wright rosettes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Homer wright rosettes are seen in Neuroblastoma.
